index.001: RAID Calculator for iPhone, iPad and Android
index.009: How much space will you actually get?
index.010: RAID Calculator for iPhone, iPad and Android shows your usable capacity, how many drives can fail, and which drive to buy next, whether your NAS runs Synology, Unraid, ZFS, SnapRAID or Btrfs.
index.012: Most calculators assume identical drives. Your NAS has a 4 TB from 2019 next to last month’s 16 TB.
index.014: Set each bay’s drive size or leave it empty. Every drive is drawn to scale and split into what it actually holds: data, parity, a mirror copy, or nothing at all.
index.016: Switch between Synology, Unraid, ZFS, SnapRAID and Btrfs RAID1 and watch the same bays re-split. Compare Systems lines them all up, most usable space first, and says when a system reads fewer bays than you set up, or more than the one you’re viewing.
index.018: Unused capacity is hatched, with the number spelled out: “8 TB unused with this mix of drives.”
index.020: Biggest Upgrade names the single purchase that unlocks the most space: “Replace bay 4 (4 TB) with 16 TB, +12 TB usable.” One tap tries it.
index.022: Save as Current Setup once, and every later change is measured against it (“+4 TB usable”), with Revert to go back.
index.026: Upgrading one drive in an SHR array often gains less than you’d expect until a second large drive joins it. The app shows that number before you spend.
index.027: 8, 4, 8 and 8 TB drives in SHR on iPad, with every system compared and the gain over the saved setup.
index.028: Pick a bay count from 2 to 12 for Synology, or up to 30 for Unraid, ZFS, SnapRAID and Btrfs RAID1. SHR and SHR-2 sit alongside Synology’s RAID 1, 5 and 6. Unraid and SnapRAID put parity on your largest drives automatically, and for ZFS the app also shows the figure ZFS will report, labeled as an estimate.
index.029: RAID 0 to 60, RAID-Z and JBOD. The answer first, the reasoning right under it.
index.030: Set the number of drives (1–24) and a size in GB or TB. Usable capacity is the biggest thing on screen, with raw capacity and efficiency beneath it. Your last setup is remembered. Nested levels and RAID-Z show their groups, and RAID-Z adds what ZFS itself will report.
index.031: See why RAID 10 costs half your drives
index.032: One bar per drive, colored by what it does: data, parity or mirror, so the mirrored pairs are plain to see. Fault tolerance is honest about the conditional cases: “Up to 4 (depends on which drives fail).”
index.033: A warning while it still matters
index.034: RAID 5, RAID 50 and RAID-Z1 on drives of 8 TB or more warn that a rebuild can take days and that a second failure during it loses the array. When the groups are wide enough to move up, one tap switches to RAID 6, RAID 60 or RAID-Z2.
index.036: “RAID 6 requires at least 4 drives.” Tap “Use 4 drives” and the numbers come back. Every level and every NAS system has an info sheet: overview, pros, cons and typical uses, plus ratings for RAID levels and how the app calculates RAID-Z and each NAS system.
index.037: Speed and availability ratings compare RAID levels with each other; they aren’t benchmarks. Capacity uses the standard simplified formulas, and the app also shows the figure most NAS systems report (“≈ 58.2 TiB”).
index.038: Native SwiftUI on iPhone and iPad. Light mode, dark mode, eleven languages.
index.039: Liquid Glass, Dynamic Type at every size including the largest accessibility sizes, and VoiceOver that reads diagrams as full sentences: “Bay 1, 16 TB: 8 TB parity, 8 TB unused.” It also reads each drive within a group. English, Spanish, French, Italian, Japanese, German, Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese, Korean, Brazilian Portuguese and Russian.
index.041: Results beside inputs, every system compared at a glance, and up to 30 bays on screen at once. It adapts to split view too.
index.043: Closed, the outer display shows a single column beside the system’s side bars. Opened in landscape, results sit beside inputs with the fold in the gap between them, and a level’s or system’s info opens in place of the inputs, so the results stay in view.
index.047: RAID Calculator for Android is on Google Play now. It has the same RAID and NAS tabs, Compare Systems, Biggest Upgrade and Current Setup, built natively with Material 3, in eleven languages.
index.050: Two panes on foldables and tablets
index.051: On a tablet or an unfolded foldable, results sit beside the inputs. On a foldable the panes split at the fold, so nothing sits on the crease.
index.053: Like the iPhone app, it makes no network calls. On Android it doesn’t even ask for permission to use the internet.
index.054: No account, no analytics, no network calls.
index.055: Every calculation happens on your device, so the app works in a server room or anywhere else with no signal. The App Store privacy label reads Data Not Collected, and there are no third-party services.
index.061: No network calls; works fully offline
index.065: Synology Hybrid RAID builds RAID in layers of matching capacity, so mixed drive sizes waste less space than classic RAID. The app supports SHR and SHR-2, and lets you compare them with classic RAID on the same drives.
index.067: On identical drives: RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 50 and 60, JBOD, and ZFS RAID‑Z1, Z2 and Z3. With mixed drives, bay by bay: Synology SHR and SHR‑2, Unraid, ZFS, SnapRAID and Btrfs RAID1.
index.068: Why does my NAS show less than I expected?
index.069: Drives are sold in TB and most NAS systems report TiB. RAID Calculator shows both, so the number on the page matches the number you see after setup. For ZFS it also estimates what ZFS itself will report after padding and reserved space, and labels it an estimate.
index.071: Synology expansion units, SSD cache, and Unraid’s separate pools outside its main array aren’t covered. It doesn’t estimate cost, power or IOPS, and it never touches your actual disks.
index.073: No. Speed and availability are 1–5 star comparisons between RAID levels, labeled as such in the app. Capacity figures use standard simplified formulas and don’t account for a specific filesystem’s overhead, apart from the labeled ZFS estimate. NAS systems get no stars at all, since their speed depends on how each one is set up.
index.074: Know what you’ll get before you buy the drive.

privacy.011: RAID Calculator collects nothing. Every calculation happens on your device, and nothing you enter is sent anywhere.
privacy.012: This policy describes how RAID Calculator (“the App”) handles information when you use it, on iPhone and iPad (from the App Store) and on Android (from Google Play). RAID Calculator is developed and operated by mrBallistic (“we,” “us” or “our”).
privacy.014: We do not collect, store or share any personal data from you. Specifically:
privacy.015: We do not collect your name, email address or other contact information
privacy.016: We do not collect device identifiers
privacy.017: We do not collect location data
privacy.018: We do not collect usage analytics or telemetry
privacy.019: We do not receive your configurations, drive sizes, saved setups or any other values you enter into the App
privacy.020: We do not use cookies or similar tracking technologies
privacy.021: Your last configuration, and any setup you save, is stored only on your device so the App can restore it. It is never sent to us or anyone else.
privacy.022: If you have turned on your device’s own backup (for example, backup to your Google account on Android), your device may include that saved configuration in its backup, so it can return when you restore or move to a new device. That backup is handled by your device’s platform under your account. We never receive it and cannot read it.
privacy.023: All calculations are performed locally on your device. The data you enter never leaves your device as part of the App’s functionality.
privacy.031: Because we do not use these services, they cannot collect any data about your use of the App through us.
privacy.033: Because the App does not collect any personal data, it does not knowingly collect information from children under 13 (or under the age required in your jurisdiction). If you believe a child has provided us with personal information, please contact us through the contact form on mrballistic.com. However, in the normal use of the App, no data is sent to us at all.
privacy.035: Since we do not collect or store any personal data, there is nothing for you to access, correct or delete. If you have questions about this policy, you can always reach us through the contact form on mrballistic.com.
privacy.037: We may update this policy from time to time. Any changes will be posted on this page with an updated “Last updated” date. Your continued use of the App after changes are posted constitutes your acceptance of the revised policy.
privacy.039: This policy covers the App. The website you’re reading is separate: if you accept analytics cookies, it uses Google Analytics to count visits and see which pages people read. If you decline, Google’s code isn’t loaded at all and no analytics cookies are set. You can change your choice at any time with “Cookie settings” at the bottom of each page. Nothing from the App is ever sent to the website, and the App itself makes no network calls. On Android, the App does not even request permission to use the internet.
